gpt-oss-20b on CPU with vLLM: serving benchmark report

2× Xeon 6972P (192 cores, SNC3 → 6 NUMA nodes of 32 cores, 1.5 TB), vLLM 0.30.0 CPU wheel, bf16 activations with MXFP4 MoE weights. Generated from results/ by report.py.

Key findings and deployment guidance

Short version. For interactive use up to about 32 concurrent users, run one TP4 instance, adding DFlash if load stays at 16 users or fewer. For 64+ users or long prompts, run three TP2 replicas (or TP4 + TP2) behind vllm-router, with --max-num-seqs sized to the load.

Recommended deployments

ScenarioDeploymentWhat you getWhy
Latency-sensitive chat, ≤16 concurrent users TP4 + DFlash (k=7) 106–116 tok/s/user at 1 user; 60–68 at 8 users DFlash gives 1.3–1.5× per-user speed below 16 users (acceptance length 3.2–3.6) with unchanged GSM8K accuracy (93.2%).
General chat, up to ~32 concurrent users TP4 (no speculation), prefix caching on 84 tok/s/user at 1 user, 29 at 32; ~900 tok/s total Fastest single instance at every load ≤32; DFlash is break-even at 32 users.
High concurrency (64–128 users), decode-heavy TP2 ×3 or TP4 + TP2 behind the router, --max-num-seqs ≥ users per replica 1,800–1,935 tok/s at 128 users, 16–17 tok/s/user Uses all 6 NUMA nodes; TP4 alone uses 4 of them. Beats single TP4 (1,883) on throughput and TTFT.
Long prompts, short answers (RAG, summarization) TP2 ×3 1,054 tok/s at 128 users vs 688 for TP4 (+53%); TTFT 3.1 s vs 4.8 s Prompt processing parallelizes across independent engines.
Shared system prompts / few-shot templates Keep prefix caching on (default) +17–29% throughput and −17–25% TTFT at 32 users with a 512-token shared prefixShared prefix is computed once per instance.

What drives per-user speed

  • Concurrency is the main lever. On TP4, per-user speed falls from 84 tok/s (1 user) to 29 (32 users) to 15 (128 users) on decode-heavy work, while total throughput rises from 84 to 1,880 tok/s.
  • Prompt length matters at load. At 32 users, 128-token prompts give 29–31 tok/s/user, but 2048-token prompts give 13, because every step also processes other users' prefills. At 128 users with 2048-token prompts, users see only 4 tok/s and 9 s TTFT on a single TP4.
  • Content doesn't. ShareGPT prompts track random prompts of the same length within about 6%.

Configuration guidance

  • Size --max-num-seqs to the expected load per instance. With 32, TP4 plateaus at about 900 tok/s beyond 32 users and TTFT climbs to 28–83 s because requests queue. With 128 it reaches 1,880 tok/s at 1.1 s TTFT. Below 32 users, smaller values (8 or 16) only cap throughput.
  • --max-num-batched-tokens barely matters (1,024–8,192 change throughput by a few percent). 2,048 slightly lowers TTFT; 8,192 raises it.
  • Parallelism for one instance: TP4 > TP2 > TP2×PP3 > pure PP. Pipeline parallelism halves per-user speed. Expert and data parallelism currently fail on CPU (see Issues).
  • Speculative decoding is a low-load feature. DFlash raises throughput 1.25–1.74× at ≤16 users, is neutral at 32 and costs 25–28% at 64–128 users. Its gain is capped by memory bandwidth: verifying 8 tokens activates about 21 of 32 experts per MoE layer (≈2–2.4 forward passes of cost), and the drafter costs another half step.

Replicas and routing

  • Replicas win only once each replica has enough users to batch. At ≤32 users, TP4 gives the best per-user speed. TP1 ×6 is the weakest layout: 43 tok/s/user at low load and 21 at 32 users.
  • Homogeneous replicas: prefer round-robin or load-based routing. Cache-aware routing changed multi-turn throughput by −10% to +4% on equal replicas and was worse at 128 users (TP2 ×3: 1,269 vs 1,353; TP1 ×6: 889 vs 987), because conversation affinity piles load onto some replicas.
  • Mixed replica sizes: cache-aware routing helps. It balances by load, while round-robin overloads the small replicas: TP4 + TP1 ×2 gains +23% at 32–64 users.
  • Among mixed layouts, TP4 + TP2 is the only good one, matching TP4 at low load and TP2 ×3 at high load. Layouts with TP1 replicas lag.
Caveats. Per-user speed is the decode rate after the first token (1000 / TPOT). Points with few requests are noisy (±5–10%), notably MT-Bench at 32–64 users (80 prompts) and HumanEval at 128 users (164 prompts). Results come from one machine with NUMA balancing on. The vLLM wheel carries two local patches needed for DFlash on CPU.

1. Method

  • tok/s per user = 1000 / mean time per output token (TPOT), the decode speed each user sees after the first token. TTFT is reported separately. Total throughput = output tokens / wall time.
  • Concurrency = number of simultaneous users (closed loop). 4 prompts per user up to 32 users, 2 per user at 64 and 128 (at least 8).
  • Prefix caching on; the cache is reset before every point, so points never reuse each other's prompts. Random and ShareGPT runs force exact output lengths (--ignore-eos); ShareGPT prompts are filtered to ±20% of the target input length.
  • Server: --max-model-len 4096 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096, --max-num-seqs 32 up to 32 users and 128 above. KV cache 40 GB per instance, OpenMP threads bound per NUMA node.
  • Replicas: one vllm serve per replica on disjoint NUMA nodes, behind vllm-router (cache-aware policy unless stated).
  • Speculative decoding: DFlash drafter z-lab/gpt-oss-20b-DFlash, 7 draft tokens, chat endpoint, greedy decoding, real output lengths.

7. Issues found

  • Expert parallelism crashes on CPU: CPUExpertsMxfp4 ignores expert_map and passes global expert IDs to a kernel holding only local experts (out-of-bounds write in moe_align_block_size).
  • Data parallelism on CPU fails: all_gatherv is not implemented; with 6 EP ranks the MXFP4 loader also fails because 32 experts don't divide by 6.
  • DFlash on gpt-oss needs the CPU Triton fallbacks from PR #58217 and a KV-cache group-size override (the drafter's layers are split across groups otherwise). --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager corrupts gpt-oss output on CPU (GSM8K 61.6%).
  • benchmarks/multi_turn: inverted English-only filter in the ShareGPT converter, crash on conversations ending with a user turn, hang at exit, early stop by default, and TTFT/token counting that ignores reasoning output.
